summary: Specifies an architecture and gateway-to-gateway protocol to provide Fibre Channel fabric functionality over an IP network. It uses TCP for Fibre Channel frame transport and supports the Fibre Channel distributed fabric services. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Storage gear that talks Fibre Channel can only reach its neighbors. This memo uses gateways to carry its messages over the regular internet so far-away storage can connect.

questions: how does ifcp carry fibre channel over ip
what is the difference between ifcp address translation and transparent mode
subtitle: Gateways that carry Fibre Channel storage traffic across ordinary TCP/IP networks.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel storage devices normally talk through Fibre Channel switches, which limits how far apart they can be and how large a storage network can grow.
tldr.mechanism: iFCP gateways sit in front of Fibre Channel devices, wrap each Fibre Channel frame for TCP, and create one TCP connection per pair of communicating ports. An iSNS server handles discovery and configuration.
tldr.outcome: Existing Fibre Channel devices can be joined over an IP network without changing them. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 6172 and RFC 7146.

today: RFC 4172 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it was later updated by RFC 6172 and RFC 7146, so read it together with those documents.

sections.title: What iFCP Is
sections.content:
iFCP is a gateway-to-gateway protocol that provides Fibre Channel fabric services to Fibre Channel devices over a TCP/IP network. It uses TCP for congestion control, error detection and recovery. Its primary objective is to interconnect existing Fibre Channel devices at wire speeds over an IP network.

The gateways are transparent. Normal Fibre Channel frame traffic passes through a gateway directly, and the gateway intercepts and emulates the fabric services a device needs only where necessary. The RFC states that the authoritative information on Fibre Channel itself is in the T10 and T11 standards, and that the authoritative parts of this document are the mapping to TCP/IP, mainly Section 5.
sections.eli5: iFCP is a pair of translators. The storage machines keep talking as usual, and the translators carry their words across the internet and hand them to the machine at the other end.

sections.title: Fibre Channel Concepts Behind iFCP
sections.content:
Fibre Channel is a frame-based, serial technology for peer-to-peer communication between devices at gigabit speeds with low overhead and latency. Its end points are N_PORTs, which attach to the network through fabric ports. Topologies are arbitrated loop, switched fabric, or a mixed fabric of switches and loops.

A frame has a header, a payload of 0 to 2112 bytes and a 32-bit CRC, bracketed by start-of-frame (SOF) and end-of-frame (EOF) delimiters. The header carries 24-bit source and destination fabric addresses (S_ID and D_ID), made of a Domain ID, an Area ID and a Port ID. Domain IDs run from 1 to 239.

A device acquires its address when it logs in to the fabric, so addresses are volatile. Three logins exist: Fabric Login (FLOGI), Port Login (PLOGI) and Process Login (PRLOGI). A switched fabric must provide an F_PORT server, a Fabric Controller and a Directory/Name Server. Of the transport classes, classes 2 and 3 are the ones most used for storage, and class 3 is described as similar to UDP or IP datagram service.
sections.eli5: Fibre Channel is like a private road system for storage machines, where every machine has a street address that the road system hands out when it arrives. The addresses can change, so machines look each other up before talking.

sections.title: Gateways, Regions and iSNS
sections.content:
In an iFCP network, IP components replace the Fibre Channel switching and routing infrastructure. Each gateway region is the part of the fabric reached through one iFCP gateway. Looking into its fabric port, the gateway appears as a Fibre Channel switch element and remote N_PORTs look like fabric-attached devices. On the IP side, it presents each local N_PORT as a logical Fibre Channel device. The RFC compares each region to an autonomous system whose configuration is invisible to the IP network and to other regions.

iFCP supports class 2 and class 3 service, and does not support class 4, class 6 or class 1.

Discovery and management use the Internet Storage Name Service (iSNS), and access to an iSNS server is required. It emulates the Fibre Channel name server, groups gateways into fabrics, segments a fabric into zones through discovery domains, stores security policies, and supports broadcast. Each gateway MUST also provide the F_PORT server, Fabric Controller and Directory/Name Server at their well-known addresses, and MAY provide a broadcast server. A name server request from a device is translated into an iSNS query.
sections.eli5: Each storage room has a doorman (the gateway) who pretends to be the whole road system to the machines inside. A phone book service (iSNS) tells the doormen where everyone else lives.

sections.title: Address Translation and Address Transparent Modes
sections.content:
Gateways run in one of two modes. In address translation mode, an N_PORT address is local to its gateway region. The gateway gives each remote N_PORT a local 24-bit N_PORT alias. Outbound frames are encapsulated and sent unmodified. The receiving gateway fills in the D_ID with the real destination N_PORT ID and the S_ID with the alias it assigned, then recalculates the Fibre Channel CRC. Fabrics built this way are called unbounded, and are not limited by Fibre Channel address allocation across regions.

In address transparent mode, addresses are unique across a bounded iFCP fabric, using Domain IDs issued by the iSNS server from a common pool. No translation takes place. This is limited to a combined total of 239 gateways and switch elements.

All gateways MUST support address translation mode. Support for address transparent mode is OPTIONAL. A gateway MUST NOT change mode after it starts processing frames, run two modes at once, or form a session with a gateway in a different mode. Link service messages that carry N_PORT addresses in their payload get special handling in translation mode, with supplemental data added so the receiver can convert the addresses.
sections.eli5: In one mode, each room has its own street numbers, and the doorman swaps numbers on every letter. In the other mode, everyone shares one big numbering scheme, so no swapping is needed, but the scheme runs out sooner.

sections.title: iFCP Sessions over TCP
sections.content:
An iFCP session is a pair of N_PORTs joined by a single TCP connection. No more than one session SHALL exist between a given pair of N_PORTs. A session may be started by a PLOGI. A gateway may keep a pool of unbound TCP connections to cut setup time.

To create a session the gateway finds the remote N_PORT descriptor (built from an iSNS query), allocates a TCP connection to the remote gateway, sends a CBIND message and enters the OPEN PENDING state. A CBIND status of Success moves the session to OPEN. If both sides start a session at the same time, the one with the greater Source N_PORT Name wins.

Three session control messages are defined: CBIND (0xE0), UNBIND (0xE4) and LTEST (0xE5). LTEST is a heartbeat requested through the Liveness Test Interval in CBIND. A session is terminated if an LTEST is not received within twice the interval. UNBIND ends a session and, if it succeeds, the TCP connection may stay open in the pool.

For TCP features, keep alive and the Nagle algorithm should not be used, while window scaling and PAWS from RFC 1323 should be supported. Gateways aborting a session because of a wrong address mode reset the TCP connection without an UNBIND.
sections.eli5: When two machines want to talk, their doormen dial each other on a phone line (TCP) and agree 'this line is for these two only'. They can send little 'are you still there?' pings, and hang up politely when done.

sections.title: Frame Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
Each Fibre Channel frame is wrapped using the common encapsulation format of RFC 3643: a 7-word header, an SOF delimiter word, the frame including its CRC, and an EOF delimiter word. The header holds the protocol number (2 for iFCP), a version, ones-complement copies of several fields for checking, the frame length in 32-bit words, an integer and a fractional time stamp, and a header CRC that MUST be valid.

iFCP adds three flag bits: SES marks a session control frame, TRP is 1 for address transparent mode and 0 for address translation mode, and SPC marks a link service message needing special iFCP processing. Only certain start and end delimiters are allowed: SOFi2, SOFn2, SOFi3, SOFn3, EOFn and EOFt.

On receipt, the gateway checks the header CRC, the flags and the time stamp, then the delimiters and the Fibre Channel CRC. It then fills in the S_ID and D_ID if in translation mode, and forwards the frame to the N_PORT in the D_ID field.
sections.eli5: Each Fibre Channel message goes inside an envelope with a label that says who made it, how long it is and when it was sent. The receiver checks the envelope before opening it.

sections.title: Stale Frame Prevention
sections.content:
Fibre Channel recovery assumes lost frames cannot appear later. A fabric guarantees this by limiting frame lifetime to R_A_TOV, whose default is 10 seconds. A gateway SHALL enforce it using the time stamp in the encapsulation header. The IP network's share, called IP_TOV, should be set well below R_A_TOV, at 50 percent of it, and stored in the iSNS server.

Gateways keep their clocks aligned using SNTP (RFC 2030), with a resolution of 125 milliseconds or better. A gateway is either Synchronized or Unsynchronized. When synchronized, it discards incoming frames whose time in flight exceeds IP_TOV. Entering the Unsynchronized state, for example at power-up or after losing contact with the time server, aborts all iFCP sessions, and no new ones may be created until it is synchronized again.
sections.eli5: Old messages must not show up late and confuse everyone. So every message gets a timestamp, and the receiver throws away any message that took too long to arrive.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
iFCP relies on the IPsec suite for confidentiality and authentication, and on IKE for key management. The RFC lists threats such as snooping, modifying or injecting packets, hijacking the TCP connection, denial of service, impersonating a security gateway and compromising communication with the iSNS server.

Implementations MUST support ESP (RFC 2406) in tunnel mode, with per-packet origin authentication, integrity and replay protection. HMAC with SHA1 and 3DES in CBC mode MUST be implemented, NULL encryption MUST be supported, and DES in CBC mode SHOULD NOT be used. IKE MUST be supported, pre-shared key authentication is mandatory, and manual keying MUST NOT be used. Certificates MAY be supported.

Rekeying must keep up with high data rates. The RFC gives an example of rekeying as often as every 27.5 seconds at 10 Gbps. Security mechanisms may be administratively disabled for a portal, but then authentication of the iSNS server SHOULD still be used as a minimum.
sections.eli5: Because the messages cross the open internet, they are locked in a box that only the two doormen can open, and the locks are changed often.
